> 十年后，公司里或许不再需要一个专门的"软件工程师"岗位。不是说写代码没用了，而是普通人拿到结果，不再需要先造一个软件。

# 我们还需要那么多软件工程师吗？

我自己就是软件工程师，最近被一个问题缠住了：以后还需要那么多软件工程师吗？我把两个自己亲历的 case 摆在一起比了比，答案有点扎心。

### 软件工程师到底在交付什么

先说我这些年干的事。我的主职是软件工程师，产出路径很固定：架构设计、软件设计、代码设计，然后代码实现，写代码这个过程现在也是拿 Coding Agent 在写，一个 APP 由 Coding Agent 直接制作出来。代码写出来干嘛？给用户提供服务。用户买了我的软件，用它拿到自己想要的交付物，价值才算产生。说到底，我交付的是软件，软件替用户交付价值。

但我最近同时在干另一件事。我在做个人内容管理的小项目，全程用 Agent 跑，它直接给我产出文档、播客、图片这些多媒体材料，到手就是交付物。

两个 case 摆一起，范式的区别就出来了：一个产出软件，软件为人服务；另一个直接为用户服务，中间不带绕的。

### 一个绕了很久才搞懂的区别

这个概念我困惑了很久。Claude Code、Codex、GitHub Copilot、Cursor 这些 coding agent，我用得挺顺手，感觉什么都能干。那为什么还有 Claude Cowork、OpenClaw、Hermes，以及整合后的 ChatGPT、国内这些 WorkBuddy、千问办公？我始终没搞懂它们差在哪。

后来靠上面两个 case 才想通：Claude Code、Codex 这类终端工具，交付的是一个软件。可大部分用户要的根本不是软件，是结果。

顺手补两句背景。Hermes 是 Nous Research 今年 2 月推的开源自主 AI 智能体框架，中文圈叫它「爱马仕」，特色是每次任务结束自动把经验沉淀成 Skill，主打自我进化。千问办公是阿里的 AI 办公平台，一句话就能完成数据分析、PPT 生成、视频剪辑、网页搭建，直接交付成果。它俩都是直接给结果那一路。

那 CLI 工具能不能直接给结果？能，但隔着一层。Coding Agent 里写死了大量系统提示词，天生就是为构建软件准备的。用户要的是能直接用的结果时，它很难胜任。所以 Coding Agent 和 Work 类 Agent 的本质区别一句话：一个产出中间结果，再靠中间结果服务用户；另一个直接为用户产出结果。

### 交互，成了新的中间产物

既然直接给结果了，中间过程就消失了？没有，只是换了位置。以前用户操作买来或下载的软件，软件给结果；现在用户直接跟 Agent 交互拿结果，交互过程本身就成了中间产物。

这个中间产物抽象一下，就是 Agent Skill。举个具体的：每天要把需求做成 PPT 向领导汇报，频次高到一天一次。只要懂点 Agent Skill，就会把整套流程沉淀成一个 Skill，省得天天重复那几句话。这么一看，Agent Skill 变成了中间软件，Agent 变成了软件的运行平台。AI Agent 是操作系统之上更高一层的抽象运行层，Skill 就是跑在这层上面的 Application。

### 需求到结果的距离，被大大缩短

从需求端到结果交付端，中间本来要靠写个软件走完，而且这个软件多半还得第三方开发者来做。现在自己跟 AI 交互就能解决，开发者这层可以拿掉了。所以未来对软件开发的需求会大大减少，尤其是请专业软件开发者来做软件的需求。

### 软件开发不会消失，只是换了形态

但软件开发这行不会没。业务复杂到一定程度，或者要专项化加速的时候，总有一部分逻辑得固化死，只能靠代码。放 Skill 里效率不够，就得要专业程序、专业性能优化。不过这时候得想明白：这是你特定需求的产物，不是通用需求，传统软件公司未必接得住这种活。这种岗位以后长什么样，我还没想明白。

另一类还会存在的是 Agent 运行时本身，它依然需要专业软件工程师来写。但世界永远是二八法则，20% 的人开发了 80% 人用的软件，赢者通吃。我判断中国市场以后大概只剩三家专门做 Agent 运行时的公司，那也只需要三拨人，桌面端也好、基础设施也好，三家公司就够。其他公司不用自己做运行时，自然也不用养专业软件工程师。

### 真正的 AI Native，和工程师的两条出路

所以说到底，AI Native 不是拿 AI 去写代码，而是在 AI Agent 平台上构建 Skill、构建 Agent 系统，直接为用户产出结果，这才是真正的 AI Native。

顺着推，未来软件工程师的岗位需求量会大大减少。这个结论我还不敢说死，但趋势已经成形。想继续在这行干，我看只有两条出路。一条是围着用户的个性化需求转，帮他产出软件，过程由 AI Agent 辅助。至于以什么形式出现，外包也好，OpenAI 现在推的 FDE 也好，我还不确定。FDE 就是贴近客户一线、直接部署落地 AI 方案的前向部署工程师。另一条是进真正做 AI Native 的 Agent 开发商，那里还有丰富的软件开发需求和基础设施搭建维护需求。

### 这套判断，靠两个前提撑着

这套判断我还有两个前提要交代。第一，AI Native 得被验证完全可行、没有致命问题。从我的观察看，八九不离十，它已经是指数级成长的过程，这条路必定走下去。第二，绝大多数普通用户要能接受并适配这个时代，习惯直接跟 Agent 沟通拿结果。人类适应能力其实很强。当年微软推 Office，没人会打字；Word 成熟普及后，现在所有人都打字。这个范式变化，我赌也会被绝大多数人习惯。

> 如果 AI Native 真成了，十年后公司里的"软件工程师"，可能就像现在的"打字员"一样少见。别急着反驳——不是写代码没用了，而是"先做个软件再拿结果"这条路，对大多数人来说没必要了。

最近我一直在想一个问题：我们还需要那么多软件工程师吗？

问出这个问题的，恰恰是我自己——一个在职的软件工程师。听起来有点像在砸自己的饭碗。🤔

但我是认真的。最近，我一边自己捣鼓点个人项目，一边观察身边工具的变化，越来越觉得：软件工程师这个岗位，可能要变天了。

## 交付一个软件，还是交付一个结果？

先说说我的日常。

我的主职是软件工程师。以前我的产出物是什么？是根据设计，做架构设计、软件设计、代码设计，然后做代码实现。我交付的，是一个软件。

但这个软件的根本目的是什么？说白了，是为了卖给用户，用户用它去拿到自己想要的东西，从而产生价值。

换句话说：我交付软件，软件再为用户交付价值。这中间，是隔着一层的。

以前我没觉得这有什么问题。直到最近，我自己做一些个人内容管理相关的小项目，事情开始变得不一样了。

## 两个 case，让我看清范式在变

第一个 case：我用 Coding Agent 去写代码，制作一个 APP。Coding Agent 帮我产出的，是一个软件。

第二个 case：我直接用 Agent 去做内容，它直接产出了我要的文档、我要的播客、我要的图片，这些多媒体材料。

你看，一个是"产生软件，软件为人服务"，另一个是"直接为用户服务"。这就是范式上的区别。

用户要的从来不是一个软件，用户要的是一个结果。这个道理，以前我只是嘴上说说，现在是真的看懂了。

## Coding Agent 和 Work 类 Agent，到底差在哪

我之前一直对一堆工具的区别很困惑。

我一直用 Claude Code、Codex、GitHub Copilot、Cursor 这些 coding agent，用得很好，觉得它们可以用来做任何事情。那为什么还需要 Claude Cowork、OpenClaw、Hermes，甚至整合后的 ChatGPT，还有国内的 WorkBuddy、千问办公？

这个困惑，靠对比上面两个 case，我慢慢解开了。

Hermes 是 Nous Research 开源的一个自主 Agent 框架，主打自我进化，跑完一次任务会自动把经验沉淀成 Skill，中文圈有人戏称"养马"。千问办公则是阿里的一站式 AI 办公平台，一句话就能完成数据分析、PPT 生成、视频剪辑这些活，直接交付成果。

这些工具和传统 coding agent 不是一类东西。像 Claude Code、Codex 这种终端工具，它的交付物是软件。而绝大部分用户要的，是直接的结果。这是最大的区别，本质上是一次范式转移。

那 CLI 工具能不能直接给用户结果？答案是可以的。但你要明白，Coding Agent 里写死了大量系统提示词，这些提示词天然是为"创建构建一个软件"而存在的。当用户需要的是一个直接给出结果的产品时，Coding Agent 并不能很好地胜任。

所以 Coding Agent 和 Work 类 Agent 的本质区别在于：一个产出中间结果，通过中间结果为用户服务；另一个直接为用户产出结果。

## 交互本身，正在变成中间产物

好了，区别我们知道了。那直接让用户产出结果的时候，还有没有中间过程？

显然是有的。这个中间过程，就是我们和 Agent 交互的过程。

以前，我们是操作一个软件，软件给我一个结果。这个软件可以是买的、下载的、免费用的。现在，用户直接跟 Agent 交互，拿到想要的结果、达到想要的目的。而用户和 Agent 之间交互的过程，本身变成了一种中间产物。

再往深想一层：这种交互，最终可以抽象成 Agent Skill。

举个例子。有个需求你天天用，比如每天要把某个需求做成 PPT，向领导汇报。如果你懂一点 Agent Skill，你会把这个产出的过程沉淀成一个 Skill，以后就不用每天都重复说一遍那些话了。

那这个 Agent Skill 就变成了一个"中间的软件"，而我们的 Agent，就变成了软件的运行平台。是不是有点意思？💡

过去，中间产物直接运行在我们的操作系统上，就是那个软件，它为用户服务。现在，中间过程运行在 AI Agent 的 Runtime 上。我现在的理解是：AI Agent 是操作系统之上更上一层的抽象运行层，Skill 就是这层抽象运行层上面的一个 Application。

## 中间环节被砍掉，还需要那么多开发者吗

再进一步看。

从需求端到结果交付端，中间这个过程，通过 Agent 被大大缩短了。

以前，中间过程要写一个软件去交付，而且这个软件是由第三方开发者开发的。现在，这个过程是我们自己去实施、自己去解决、自己去跟 AI 交互的。不再依赖开发者了。

那未来对软件开发的需求，会不会大大减少？尤其是由专业软件开发人员去做这个软件的需求，我觉得会大大减少。

当然，软件开发的工作还是有的。当业务复杂到一定程度，或者需要专项化加速的时候，有一部分逻辑是固化死的，完全可以用代码来写。但你要明白，这种需求是特定需求，不是通用需求。把它交给一个专业软件工程师，是一个非常个性化的需求，不是某个通用软件产品能满足的。

传统的软件开发公司，还能满足你这样的需求吗？不一定了。那这种情况下，软件开发岗位以什么形态继续存在？说实话，我到现在还没想明白。

## 剩下谁在写代码：二八法则下的可能

还有一部分软件应用会继续存在。哪一部分？Agent 的 Runtime，Agent 的运行时，它还是需要专业化的软件工程师来写的。

但这个世界永远是二八法则：20% 的人开发了被 80% 人使用的软件，可以说是赢者通吃。我判断，接下来至少在中国市场，只会留下三家专门做 Agent 运行时的公司。

那自然而然地，你如果要 Agent，也只需要三拨人。无论是 Agent 的桌面端，还是 Agent 的 Infrastructure，三拨人、三个公司就够了。其他公司不需要做 Agent Runtime，那他们自然也不需要专业软件工程师了。

## 真正的 AI Native，不是用 AI 写代码

顺着这条线想下去，我慢慢意识到一件事。

所谓 AI Native，其实不再是用 AI 去写一个代码。我们更多是在 AI Agent 这个平台的基础上，去构建我们的 Skill、构建我们的 Agent 系统，做到直接为用户产出结果。这才是真正的 AI Native。

## 软件工程师的两条出路

如果这个趋势成立，那结论就很清楚了：未来对软件工程师岗位的需求量，会大大减少。

这是一个我还不是特别成熟的结论，但我觉得，趋势已经形成了。

如果还想继续干这个职业，我目前分析下来，只有两条出路。

Ten years from now, "software engineer" might sound as old-fashioned as "typist" does today. Not because code disappears — but because the people who need a result will stop needing a software team to get it.

*Delivering software is not the same as delivering results. The second one is what AI Native is actually about.*

I'm a software engineer. That used to define my job in a pretty simple way: take a design, make an architecture, write the code, ship a product. The product is a piece of software, and the software exists so users can get whatever it is they actually want out of it. My deliverable was always the software. The value always showed up somewhere downstream, in what someone else did with it.

Lately I've been building small personal projects, mostly around personal content management. And I've noticed something I can't unsee now. When I use an agent for these projects, it doesn't hand me software. It hands me the finished thing directly. The document I wanted. The podcast episode. The image. Done. Not a tool to make the thing, but the thing itself.

Two cases. Same me, same kind of goal, completely different shape of deliverable. In one, I produce software and software serves people. In the other, I serve people directly. That gap kept nagging at me, and I've come to think it's the whole story.

**Delivering software vs delivering results**

My coding agent produces a program. The program serves users. That's an indirect chain, because users don't actually want a program. They want the outcome. The result. Ask a user why they open your app and they won't say "for the software." They'll say "to get my thing done."

For a long time I was confused about the tool landscape. I'd been using Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor. These CLI coding agents are great, I could do almost anything with them. So why did we also need Claude Cowork, OpenClaw, Hermes, the integrated ChatGPT, and the Chinese ones like WorkBuddy or QwenWork? I genuinely could not tell them apart.

Hermes is Nous Research's open-source autonomous agent framework, out since early 2026, and its whole angle is self-evolution: a writable runtime that distills whatever you do in a session into reusable skills. Same family as OpenClaw, but heavier on memory and self-improvement. QwenWork, on the other hand, is Alibaba's one-stop AI office platform, wired deep into DingTalk: you ask for data analysis, a PPT, an edited video, a web page, and it hands back the finished deliverable, on desktop and in the browser.

Once I sat those two groups next to each other, the distinction clicked. The terminal tools deliver a program. The work agents deliver the result the user asked for. Most users never wanted the program in the first place. That's not a small difference. That's a paradigm shift.

**Why the terminal agents can't just give you results**

Can the old CLI agents produce these deliverables directly? Sure, sometimes they can. But there's a reason it doesn't work that well. Coding agents carry a huge pile of baked-in system prompts, and those prompts exist to build software. That's their entire wiring. When what you need is a product that hands a result straight to a user, a coding agent is fighting its own defaults. Not because it's weak. Because it's shaped around a different output.

So the question shifts. When an agent produces results directly, is there still an intermediate process? Of course there is. The process is the interaction itself: you talk to the agent, it works, you get the thing. From the user's side, the old loop was "operate a software product I bought, downloaded, or used for free." The new loop is "talk to an agent and get the result." The interaction has become the intermediate product.

**The interaction becomes the intermediate product**

And if the interaction is the intermediate product, it can be abstracted. That's exactly what an Agent Skill is. Picture someone with one high-frequency need: every day, they have to turn a requirement into a PPT and present it to their boss. Daily. If that person knows about Agent Skills, they package the whole routine into one skill, and stop repeating the same instructions every morning. A daily interaction turns into a one-shot call.

Here's the shift I keep coming back to: that skill is effectively a piece of software now, and the agent is the platform it runs on.

It helped me to think in layers. Before, we built an intermediate artifact, a program, that ran directly on top of the operating system and served the user. Now the user interacts with an AI agent directly, and the intermediate process runs on the agent's runtime instead. So the AI agent is an abstraction layer one level above the operating system, and a Skill is an application living on that layer. Software didn't disappear. It moved up a floor.

**The developer in the middle starts to disappear**

Follow the chain from the demand side to the delivery side. That middle stretch used to require writing a program, usually developed by a third-party developer. Now you implement it yourself: you talk to the agent, you iterate, you get the result. The middle shrinks, and the dependency on a professional developer shrinks with it.

So yes, I think demand for software development, and especially demand for professionally built software, is going to shrink a lot. That's the uncomfortable part. But it's not nothing that survives. Two pockets do, and they're different from each other.

**The software work that survives**

First, software development still exists when the business problem gets complex enough, or when you need specialist speed. Some logic is just fixed, and fixed logic is better expressed as code. But here's the key point: once you hit that point, you're talking about a specific personalized requirement, not a general one. It's not something a generic software product can satisfy. Can a traditional software company still serve you there? Maybe not. What form does that kind of development take then, and what does the job look like? I honestly haven't figured that out yet.

Second, the agent runtime and infrastructure still need real software engineers. That layer doesn't build itself. But here's the uncomfortable part. The world runs on the 80/20 rule: twenty percent of the people build the software that eighty percent use. Winner takes most. If I'm right about that, China alone will probably end up with around three companies owning the agent runtime. Desktop client, infrastructure, all of it, three shops. If you need an agent runtime, you need those three teams. Everyone else doesn't build a runtime, which means everyone else doesn't need professional software engineers either.

**What AI Native actually means**

So here's the definition I landed on. AI Native isn't "use AI to write code faster." It's building Skills and agent systems on top of an AI agent platform, so the whole thing produces results for users directly. The code, when there is any, is plumbing. The deliverable is the outcome.

**A conclusion I'm not fully sure of, and two paths if it's right**

Here's my conclusion, and I want to be honest about how firm it is. It's not fully mature yet. But the trend has formed. Demand for software engineers is going to fall a lot.

If you're a software engineer who wants to stay in this profession, I currently see two paths.

One: orbit the very personalized needs of a specific user, and help them produce their software, with an agent doing the heavy lifting. I don't know what form this takes. Outsourcing? The FDE model OpenAI keeps pushing? To be clear, FDE stands for Forward Deployed Engineer: a role that sits next to the customer, deploying and landing AI solutions in the field instead of building product features back at headquarters. Maybe that's the shape. Maybe it's something else.

Two: go work at the companies that actually do AI Native, the agent developers. That's where the rich software development demand and infrastructure work will still live.

**What has to be true for any of this to hold**

All of this rests on two assumptions, and I should say them out loud.

First, AI Native has to be genuinely implementable, no fatal flaws. From what I can see, it basically is. It's growing exponentially and maturing fast, and I'd be surprised if the road stops.

Second, ordinary users have to accept the change and adapt to living and working with agents: communicating smoothly, letting agents produce results directly. I think human adaptability is wildly underestimated here. Remember when Microsoft shipped Office? At first almost nobody could type. Then Word got better, spread everywhere, and now basically everyone can type. The next paradigm shift will feel the same. Awkward at first. Universal eventually.

I can't tell you exactly how the next five years play out, or what the job board looks like. But I can tell you the direction I'm seeing: we're moving from shipping software to shipping results, and the people who figure out that second one, users and engineers alike, are the ones who'll be fine.

前两天用 [agent-browser](https://agent-browser.dev/)（Vercel 出的、给 AI Agent 用的浏览器自动化工具）想自动化打开一个网站，结果页面死活加载不出来：要么是空白，要么提示「网络不可用 / 无法访问」。

奇怪的是——**我平时用普通 Chrome 明明能正常打开这个站**，系统代理早就配好了啊？

这事儿折腾了一圈，根因藏得挺深：既不是网站的问题，也不是 agent-browser 的 bug，而是 **Agent 的运行环境悄悄把我的代理环境变量给覆盖了**。下面把排查过程完整记下来，顺便聊聊「浏览器代理」里几个容易踩的坑。

---

## 太长不看

- **现象**：agent-browser 打开网站提示网络不可用，但本机默认 Chrome 能正常开。
- **根因（三层叠加）**：
  1. Chrome 不读 shell 里的 `HTTP_PROXY` 这类环境变量（那是 curl/wget 的约定）；
  2. agent-browser 把 Chrome 当自动化进程拉起，没自动继承 macOS 系统代理；
  3. **最隐蔽的一层**：WorkBuddy Agent 的运行环境（沙箱组件 `sandbox-c`）把 `HTTP_PROXY` 等强行注入成它自带的 `58058` 端口，而那个端口对这类请求是不通的（实测 403）。
- **解决**：给 agent-browser 显式指定真实可用的代理 `--proxy http://127.0.0.1:7892`，并设为专属变量 `AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY` 长期生效（它能避开沙箱覆盖）。

---

## 1. 先排除"反自动化拦截"

第一反应以为是网站在拦自动化浏览器。实测发现：

- headless 模式加载不出来，`--headed` 有头模式也加载不出来；
- 快照无交互元素、截图是空白的。

说明不是 headless 被识别，而是**请求根本没连通（网络不通）**。那问题大概率出在「代理没用上」。

---

## 2. 排查链路（关键证据）

### 2.1 本机到底配了什么代理

先看系统代理（macOS 网络设置）：

```bash
scutil --proxy
# HTTPProxy : 127.0.0.1
# HTTPPort  : 7892
# HTTPSProxy: 127.0.0.1
# HTTPSPort : 7892
# SOCKSProxy: 127.0.0.1
# SOCKSPort : 7892
```

这 `7892` 是你本地运行的代理工具所监听的端口。

我自己 shell 的配置（`~/.zprofile`、`~/.bash_profile`）里写的也是 `7892`：

```bash
export http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7892
export https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7892
export all_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7892
```

**但是**，在 Agent 的 Bash 执行环境里 `env | grep proxy`，看到的却是另一套：

```bash
HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:58058
HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:58058
http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:58058
https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:58058
```

注意端口从 `7892` 变成了 `58058`。问题就藏在这里。

### 2.2 实测每个端口到底通不通

光看配置不够，得实测。用 `curl` 分别试三条路（`<目标网站的 URL>` 换成你要访问的地址）：

```bash
# 直连（无代理）
curl -I -L --max-time 10 "<目标网站的 URL>"
# → HTTP/2 403（不通）

# 经本地代理 7892
curl -x http://127.0.0.1:7892 -I -L --max-time 10 "<目标网站的 URL>"
# → HTTP/2 200  ✅（连通）

# 经 Agent 环境里的 58058
curl -x http://127.0.0.1:58058 -I -L --max-time 10 "<目标网站的 URL>"
# → HTTP/2 403  ❌（不通）
```

**真相浮现**：真正可用的代理出口是 `7892`；`58058` 不通（沙箱代理不转发这类请求）。

### 2.3 58058 到底是谁配的

在 `~/.zprofile`、`~/.bash_profile`、代理配置里全文搜 `58058`——**一个字面量都没有**。它不是你写在哪个配置文件里的。

那就看这个端口现在是谁在监听：

```bash
lsof -iTCP:58058 -sTCP:LISTEN
# sandbox-c  6466  ...  TCP localhost:58058 (LISTEN)
```

`sandbox-c` 是 **WorkBuddy / CodeBuddy 工具沙箱**的组件。结论很清楚：

> **58058 不是你的配置，是 Agent 运行环境的沙箱在运行时注入的本地代理端口**，不属于任何磁盘文件，所以「去配置文件里看」是看不到的。

---

## 3. 根因分析

把三层原因叠起来看：

**① Chrome 不读 shell 代理变量**
`HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` 是 curl、wget 这类命令行工具的约定。Chrome（无论系统版还是 agent-browser 起的）**根本不认这个环境变量**。所以即便环境里有正确的 `7892`，Chrome 也用不上。

**② agent-browser 的自动化启动没自动继承 macOS 系统代理**
你平时手动打开的系统版 Chrome 是 GUI 程序，会自动读 macOS 网络设置里的系统代理——所以你能正常打开那个站点。但 agent-browser 把 Chrome 当**后台/自动化进程**拉起（带独立 profile 目录、走调试协议），这种启动方式在我们的实测里**没有自动套用系统代理**——不加 `--proxy` 时访问直接 403，加上才 200。

**③ 最隐蔽的一层：Agent 运行环境覆盖了代理变量**
WorkBuddy Agent 的 Bash 执行环境里，`sandbox-c` 把 `HTTP_PROXY` 等强行注入成它自带的 `58058`，把你 `.zprofile` 里的 `7892` 给盖掉了。这个端口对这类请求是 403 的。

> **注意区分**：你「自己的终端」里 `HTTP_PROXY` 仍是 `7892`（来自 `.zprofile`），不会被覆盖；被覆盖的是「Agent 执行命令时的运行环境」。但无论哪种情况，Chrome 本身都不读这个变量，所以 agent-browser 必须显式拿到正确的代理地址。

一句话根因：**agent-browser 启动的 Chrome 既没自动读系统代理、也不读 shell 代理变量；而 Agent 运行环境又把代理变量覆盖成了一个不通的沙箱端口 58058**——于是双重失灵，目标网站因网络没有连通而被挡住。

---

## 4. 解决方案

### 4.1 临时（单次，显式指定代理）

```bash
agent-browser --proxy "http://127.0.0.1:7892" \
  --session "my-session" --restore \
  --profile /path/to/your/browser-profile \
  --headed open "<目标网站的 URL>"
```

关键就是那个 `--proxy "http://127.0.0.1:7892"`。加上之后，目标网站就能正常加载了。

### 4.2 长期（设专属变量，避免每次写 `--proxy`，且避开沙箱覆盖）

把下面这行加进 `~/.zprofile`（和已有的代理配置放一起）：

```bash
# agent-browser 专用代理（沙箱环境会覆盖 HTTP_PROXY，故用专属变量指向真实可用的本地代理 7892）
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY="http://127.0.0.1:7892"
```

```bash
source ~/.zprofile   # 立即生效
```

之后直接 `agent-browser ... open <url>` 就不用再写 `--proxy` 了，它会自动读这个变量。

**为什么用 `AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY` 而不是 `HTTP_PROXY`？**
agent-browser 其实也认 `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY`，但在 Agent 沙箱环境里，这两个变量会被强行覆盖成失效的 `58058`。`AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY` 是 agent-browser 的**专属变量**，沙箱不会去动它，所以最稳。

---

## Background: what I was even doing

I've been using **[agent-browser](https://agent-browser.dev/)** — Vercel's browser-automation CLI built for AI agents. Instead of dumping a giant DOM, it streams a compact accessibility tree with stable `@e1` / `@e2` references, so an agent can navigate, fill forms, and click with a fraction of the tokens a traditional Playwright setup burns. So I pointed it at a site I needed to automate. The site only loads when traffic is routed through a proxy (hit it directly and you get a `403`). No big deal — my machine has a proxy configured, my everyday Chrome opens the site without thinking about it.

Except agent-browser couldn't load it. Blank page. "Network unavailable." Repeatedly.

That sent me down a rabbit hole that ended somewhere I didn't expect: not in the site, and not in agent-browser — but in **my agent runtime quietly rewriting my proxy settings out from under me.**

If you automate browser tasks from inside an AI-agent tool, this is worth ten minutes of your time.

## TL;DR

- **Symptom:** agent-browser fails to load a site; your regular GUI Chrome loads it fine.
- **Root cause is three layers stacked on top of each other:**
  1. Chrome doesn't read `HTTP_PROXY` from the shell — that's a curl/wget convention, not a Chrome one.
  2. agent-browser launches Chrome as an automation process and doesn't auto-inherit the macOS *system* proxy.
  3. **The sneaky one:** the agent's own sandbox (`sandbox-c`) injects its *own* proxy on `:58058`, overwriting your `:7892` — and that port returns `403` for these requests.
- **Fix:** tell agent-browser the proxy explicitly with `--proxy http://127.0.0.1:7892`, and make it permanent with the dedicated `AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY` environment variable (which the sandbox won't touch).

## Step 1 — Rule out "the site is blocking bots"

My first instinct was that the site detected automation and refused to serve it. So I tested both modes:

- Headless: wouldn't load.
- `--headed` (visible window): also wouldn't load.
- The accessibility snapshot had no interactive elements; the screenshot was blank.

If it were headless detection, the headed window would usually get through. Blank in *both* modes pointed somewhere else: **the request never actually connected.** That smells like "proxy not being used."

---

## Step 2 — What proxy is actually on this machine?

First, the macOS system proxy (set in Network preferences):

```bash
scutil --proxy
# HTTPProxy : 127.0.0.1
# HTTPPort  : 7892
# HTTPSProxy: 127.0.0.1
# HTTPSPort : 7892
# SOCKSProxy: 127.0.0.1
# SOCKSPort : 7892
```

`7892` is the port my local proxy tool listens on. My shell init files (`~/.zprofile`, `~/.bash_profile`) agree:

```bash
export http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7892
export https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7892
export all_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:7892
```

So far, so consistent. **But** the moment I ran the same check *inside the agent's Bash environment*, I got a different story:

```bash
env | grep proxy
# HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:58058
# HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:58058
# http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:58058
# https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:58058
```

The port had silently changed from `7892` to `58058`. That's the first real clue.

---

## Step 3 — Which port actually works?

Configs lie; tests don't. I `curl`'d the target through each candidate (`<TARGET_URL>` = the site in question):

```bash
# Direct (no proxy)
curl -I -L --max-time 10 "<TARGET_URL>"
# → HTTP/2 403   (fails)

# Through the local proxy on 7892
curl -x http://127.0.0.1:7892 -I -L --max-time 10 "<TARGET_URL>"
# → HTTP/2 200   ✅ (works)

# Through the agent environment's 58058
curl -x http://127.0.0.1:58058 -I -L --max-time 10 "<TARGET_URL>"
# → HTTP/2 403   ❌ (fails)
```

Now the picture is clear: **`7892` is the real egress; `58058` is dead for these requests.** The agent environment was handing Chrome a proxy that goes nowhere.

---

## Step 4 — Who actually owns 58058?

I grepped every shell rc file and proxy config for `58058`. **Zero hits.** It isn't something I wrote. So who's listening on it?

```bash
lsof -iTCP:58058 -sTCP:LISTEN
# sandbox-c  6466  ...  TCP localhost:58058 (LISTEN)
```

`sandbox-c` is a component of the **WorkBuddy / CodeBuddy agent sandbox**. The conclusion is unambiguous:

> **`58058` is not your configuration. It's a local proxy the agent runtime injects at runtime.** It lives in the process environment, not on disk — which is exactly why "go look in your config files" finds nothing.

---

## Root cause, all three layers

Putting it together:

1. **Chrome ignores shell proxy variables.** `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` are conventions for command-line tools like curl and wget. Chrome — whether the system build or one launched by agent-browser — never reads them. So even a *correct* `7892` in the environment does Chrome no good.
2. **Automation launches skip the system proxy.** Your GUI Chrome is a normal app and auto-reads the macOS system proxy — that's why the site opens for you by default. agent-browser launches Chrome as a background/automation process (its own profile directory, driven over a debug protocol). In our testing, that launch path did **not** auto-apply the system proxy: no `--proxy` → `403`; with it → `200`.
3. **The hidden layer:** inside the agent's Bash environment, `sandbox-c` forcibly overwrites `HTTP_PROXY` (and friends) with its own `58058`, clobbering the `7892` from your `.zprofile`. And that port returns `403`.

> Important distinction: in *your own terminal*, `HTTP_PROXY` stays `7892` (straight from `.zprofile`) and is never overridden. What gets clobbered is the *agent's execution environment*. But notice — even in your own terminal it wouldn't have helped, because Chrome doesn't read the variable in the first place. The takeaway is the same either way: **agent-browser must be told the correct proxy address explicitly.**

**One-line version:** the Chrome that agent-browser launches neither inherits the system proxy nor reads shell proxy vars — and the agent runtime overwrote the proxy var with a dead sandbox port (`58058`) — so the target site is unreachable.

## The fix

### Quick fix — pass it explicitly, every time

```bash
agent-browser --proxy "http://127.0.0.1:7892" \
  --session "my-session" --restore \
  --profile /path/to/your/browser-profile \
  --headed open "<TARGET_URL>"
```

That one flag — `--proxy "http://127.0.0.1:7892"` — is the entire fix. The site loads.

### Permanent fix — a dedicated variable that survives the sandbox

Drop this into `~/.zprofile` next to your existing proxy config:

```bash
# agent-browser proxy — the sandbox overrides HTTP_PROXY, so use the dedicated var
export AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY="http://127.0.0.1:7892"
```

```bash
source ~/.zprofile   # apply immediately
```

After that, `agent-browser ... open <url>` needs no `--proxy` — it reads `AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY` automatically.

**Why a dedicated variable instead of reusing `HTTP_PROXY`?** agent-browser *does* honor `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` — but the sandbox forcibly rewrites those to the dead `58058`. `AGENT_BROWSER_PROXY` is a *tool-specific* variable the sandbox leaves alone, so it's the stable choice. (This is the same reason I'd avoid leaning on the generic `HTTP_PROXY` at all inside an agent environment.)

## Things I learned the hard way

- **One profile directory = one session at a time.** If two Chrome instances point at the same profile, they fight over the lock and the later one gets a corrupted profile — pages just never load. Half my browser open/close churn during this debugging was simply releasing that lock.
- **Use agent-browser's native `--proxy`, not `--args --proxy-server=...`.** Passing the proxy as a raw Chrome flag broke the debug channel: Chrome came up but became uncontrollable from the CLI. Cost me a session.
- **Before trusting any config, test reachability per port:** `curl -x <port> -I <url>`. It tells you instantly which port actually works.
- **`lsof -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN` is the fastest way to distinguish "something I configured" from "something a tool or sandbox injected."** It saved this whole investigation.
- **Don't assume "the OS has a proxy, so the automation browser uses it."** Chrome's proxy sources (system settings, launch flags) and curl's (environment variables) are two entirely separate mechanisms.
- A profile directory that was first opened *without* a working proxy gets polluted by the failed "unreachable" response. When something weird persists, spin up a fresh empty directory and retry.
